name: Isometric

lumenary.blurb: A city of blocks: height follows brightness, colour follows the picture.

facts.bestOn: Pictures with clear light and dark regions, such as cityscapes

why: Isometric drawing shows three faces of a cube with no vanishing point, so every block has the same size wherever it sits. That makes it a natural way to turn a picture into a city of columns, with height following brightness. Three fixed shades on the three faces suggest a light source and give the flat blocks volume.
how: Reduce the picture to a small grid.
Make each cell a block with the cell’s colour and a height from its brightness, after an auto-levels stretch.
Draw each block as three flat faces: a top, a left side and a right side with fixed brightness multipliers.
Project with the 2:1 dimetric view, so a step on a grid axis moves half a tile across and a quarter of a tile down.
Draw blocks in order of i plus j, from back to front, and scale the city to fit.
history: William Farish formalised isometric projection at Cambridge in 1822, and engineers used it for technical drawings. Video games adopted it in the 1980s with titles such as Zaxxon and Q*bert, and city builders like SimCity 2000 in 1993 made it familiar. The 2:1 version used here keeps lines on whole pixel steps, which is why pixel artists prefer it.
terms: Greek for equal measure: a view in which all three axes are shown at equal scale.
A projection where each step moves two units across for one down, loved by pixel artists.
Brightness that depends on the angle between a surface and the light.
paragraphs: The picture is reduced to a small grid and every cell becomes a block. A block’s colour is the cell’s colour; its height is the cell’s brightness, stretched so the darkest cell in the picture is as low as the lightest is tall (an “auto-levels” step that keeps flat pictures from producing a flat city). Each block is drawn as three flat faces: a top, a left side and a right side.

The projection is the 2:1 “dimetric” used in pixel-art games, where every step along a grid axis moves half a tile across and a quarter of a tile down. It is not mathematically isometric (which would use 30° and a 1:1.15 ratio) but it keeps lines on whole-pixel steps and looks cleaner. Because there is no depth buffer, blocks are drawn in order of i + j, back to front, so nearer blocks cover farther ones. The three faces get fixed brightness multipliers, which is Lambert shading for a light at a fixed position, and the whole city is scaled to fit the canvas.

equations.note: Screen position of the top of block (i, j) with tile width w and block height h.

presets.text: Tall blocks with narrow gaps feel like a dense skyline.
Greyscale blocks look like a clean architectural model.
Make dark areas tall to invert the city.
